entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aurelius Heraclianus emerged as a pivotal, if ultimately ill-fated, military commander and praetorian prefect during the tumultuous Crisis of the Third Century (235-284 CE) in the Roman Empire. Operating in the mid-3rd century, his career was inextricably linked to the reign of Emperor Gallienus, serving as one of the emperor's most trusted, yet controversial, lieutenants. His significance lies in his deep involvement in the military campaigns against numerous usurpers and barbarian incursions that threatened the very fabric of the Roman state, ultimately culminating in his role in the dramatic events surrounding Gallienus's assassination.

Heraclianus distinguished himself through a series of military engagements, notably participating in the campaign against the usurpers Macrianus Major and his sons Quietus and Macrianus Minor, who had challenged Gallienus's authority from the East in 261 CE. His command experience was crucial in securing the loyalty of key legions and orchestrating tactical maneuvers against these internal threats. However, his most infamous act was his alleged involvement in the conspiracy that led to the assassination of Emperor Gallienus during the siege of Mediolanum (modern Milan) in 268 CE, where the emperor was attempting to suppress the usurpation of Aureolus. Following Gallienus's death, Heraclianus was himself swiftly executed, highlighting the brutal and precarious nature of power during this era of rapid imperial succession.
